n: T

- *Paul, a prisoner*: Tradition says the apostle Paul was writing from prison in Rome. But he might have written it earlier from Ephesus, which is closer to Philemon’s home in Colossae (see Philemon Book Introduction, “Date and Place of Writing”).

- *Timothy: *He was one of Paul’s closest fellow workers (see “Timothy” Profile). 

- *fellow worker*: Philemon was active in ministry for Christ.
T
The apostle Paul usually begins his letters with a brief introduction. He then offers greetings and calls for grace and peace.
B

Many people wanted to stop Paul from spreading the good news about Jesus. That is why he had been put in jail.

He greeted Philemon as his dear friend and brother. They worked together as partners to spread the good news and to strengthen God’s people. Philemon was faithful to Jesus and showed love to others. This filled Paul with thanks and joy.

Philemon and Paul loved each other very much. Paul didn’t want to use his authority as an apostle to give Philemon a command. Instead, he asked Philemon to do something based on their love for one another.

Paul asked Philemon not to punish Onesimus. In Paul’s time Philemon had the right to put Onesimus to death. This was because Onesimus was Philemon’s slave and he had run away. But Paul wanted Philemon to receive Onesimus back.

Onesimus had helped take care of Paul while Paul was in prison. He had become as close to Paul as a son is to a father. Paul wanted Philemon to treat Onesimus not as a slave but as a brother. Onesimus could be as dear to Philemon as Paul was. This was because Philemon and Onesimus were now brothers in God’s family. They could be brought back together in peace because they belonged to Jesus.

Paul was willing to pay Philemon for anything that Onesimus had taken from him or done wrong. Paul also wanted Philemon to treat Onesimus the same way that he would treat Paul. This showed how closely Paul was joined to Onesimus. It was as close as how Jesus described being joined to his disciples in Matthew 10:40–42. Paul trusted that Philemon would do even more than what Paul asked. This showed Paul’s hope that Philemon would set Onesimus free.
T

- This letter is not just for Philemon, it is also for his family and the church that met in their home. 

- Apphia was probably Philemon’s wife.

- *our fellow soldier*: This refers to a servant of Christ who is in a spiritual battle and must be ready to fight against challenges ({{Ephesians 6:10-17|Ephesians 6:10–17}}).

- Archippus was probably Philemon’s son (also mentioned in {{Colossians 4:17|Colossians 4:17}}). 

- *the church that meets in your house*: This confirms that some early Christians would gather in private homes for worship (see also {{Romans 16:5|Romans 16:5}}; {{1 Corinthians 16:19|1 Corinthians 16:19}}; {{Colossians 4:15|Colossians 4:15}}).
T

- *You* is plural, referring to everyone mentioned in {{Philemon 2|1:2}}.

- *Grace and peace*: This is a traditional Greek and Hebrew greeting. They are now understood as gifts from God (compare {{Romans 5:1-2|Romans 5:1–2}}).
T

In his letters, Paul usually thanks God for the faith and love of the people he writes to. He also tells them that he prays for them ({{Romans 1:8-12|Romans 1:8–12}}; {{1 Corinthians 1:4-9|1 Corinthians 1:4–9}}; {{2 Corinthians 1:3-11|2 Corinthians 1:3–11}}; contrast {{Galatians 1:6-10|Galatians 1:6–10}}). Ancient Greek letters sometimes included a thanksgiving section after the greeting.
T
It is by faith in Christ that we are saved, and it is by love for fellow Christians that we live out our salvation.
T

You can translate this verse in different ways. Paul is hinting that Philemon should be gracious toward Onesimus because God has been good to Philemon (compare {{Philemon 10|1:10}}, {{Philemon 17-19|17–19}}).
T

- The apostle Paul asked for a favor because Philemon was well-known as a kind and loving person ({{Philemon 5-7|1:5–7}}). Paul could have used his authority as an apostle of Christ to demand it, but he chose to ask out of love.

- *I, Paul, am now aged*: Paul appealed to the respect owed to older people and his status as *a prisoner for Christ Jesus*, which would increase a fellow Christian’s respect.
T

- In the Roman world, owners could be harsh towards slaves who ran away. They could whip, mark, or even execute them.

- Onesimus was Paul's spiritual child because he became a Christian through Paul's ministry.
T

- Onesimus means “useful.” 

- *Formerly he was useless, but now he has become useful*: This might be a play on words (compare {{Philemon 20|1:20}}). Onesimus was now serving others and sharing the good news about Jesus. At last he had become what his name means.
T

Paul suggests that he wants Philemon to decide to free Onesimus so he can help Paul (also {{Philemon 21|1:21}}). The Christian life is a voluntary response to God's grace ({{Romans 12:1|Romans 12:1}}; {{Ephesians 4:1|Ephesians 4:1}}; {{Colossians 3:12-13|Colossians 3:12–13}}).
T

- *He was separated from you* (literally *he went away*): This may be a polite way of saying that Onesimus ran away. Paul might be avoiding a direct mention of what Onesimus did.

- *so that you might have him back for good*: Paul implies that God guided these events so that Onesimus would come to faith.
T

- Even though Onesimus was still legally Philemon’s slave, Philemon should consider him a beloved brother and care for his well-being.

- *both in person and in the Lord*: They were spiritual brothers in Christ so this should now change their entire relationship in both the natural and spiritual worlds.
T
Onesimus might have stolen some things from Philemon’s home or had a debt to pay off when he ran away.
T

- Paul guarantees his promise by adding his own signature. He usually dictated his letters to a secretary, but at times he wrote a short part in his own handwriting, as he does here.

- *your very self*: This means Philemon’s salvation. Philemon owed Paul far more than anything Onesimus might have owed him. It is not clear whether Paul led Philemon to faith directly or whether Philemon believed through Paul’s wider preaching (compare {{Colossians 1:7|Colossians 1:7}}).
T

*let me have some benefit*: Or do *me this favor*. The Greek word *onaimēn* (meaning “favor” or “benefit”) may be a wordplay on the name Onesimus, which can mean “useful” or “beneficial” (compare {{Philemon 11|1:11}}).
T
Paul may be suggesting that he hopes Philemon will set Onesimus free (see {{Philemon 13-14|1:13–14}}). He may also be expressing his trust in Philemon’s kindness.
T
Paul asked for a guest room because he planned to visit. This request supported his plea for Philemon to treat Onesimus kindly. When Paul arrived, he would see how Philemon would treat Onesimus.
T
Epaphras was a native of Colossae who first brought the good news to Philemon and his family ({{Colossians 1:7|Colossians 1:7}}; {{Colossians 4:12|4:12}}).
T

Paul often ends his letters with greetings from others and a blessing. Compare {{Colossians 4:7-18|Colossians 4:7–18}}. Paul’s letters to the Colossians and to Philemon were probably carried to Colossae at the same time by Tychicus and Onesimus.
T

- Paul mentions these men at the end of his letter to the Colossians ({{Colossians 4:10|Colossians 4:10}}, {{Colossians 4:14|14}}). 

- *fellow workers*: They helped the apostle Paul spread the good news about Jesus.

- *Mark*: See “John Mark” Profile.

- *Aristarchus: *He was a faithful helper who served with Paul for many years ({{Acts 19:29|Acts 19:29}}; {{Acts 20:4|20:4}}; {{Acts 27:2|27:2}}).

- *Demas*: He was a fellow worker who later abandoned Paul ({{2 Timothy 4:10|2 Timothy 4:10}}).

- *Luke*: See “Luke” Profile.
